quote: Humans may have evolved a structure of political revolution, beginning by believing themselves morally superior to the corrupt current power structure, but ending by being corrupted by power themselves
content: This is an adaptationist story with no evidence offered for any of the things an adaptation claim requires: heritable variation, cross-cultural universality, developmental specificity, or design features that would be improbable under a general-purpose account. Williams's criteria for inferring adaptation, which this book endorses elsewhere in Book III, are not met by "one can imagine ancestors who did this and reproduced." A far cheaper explanation is available and is not considered: whoever holds power faces different incentives and information than whoever seeks it, so behaviour changes on taking office without any dedicated circuitry. The essay is here doing what its neighbours in Book III warn against — reasoning from the fact that a story would explain the observation to the conclusion that it does.

quote: The tendency to be corrupted by power is a specific biological adaptation, supported by specific cognitive circuits, built into us by our genes for a clear evolutionary reason.
content: No circuit, gene, or comparative evidence is named, and the experimental literature that appeared to support "power corrupts" has fared badly: the power-priming paradigm belongs to the social-priming family that largely failed to replicate, and the best-known result in this specific area, Lammers, Stapel, and Galinsky's "Power Increases Hypocrisy" (Psychological Science 21, 2010), was retracted in the wake of the Stapel fraud investigation. Sturm and Antonakis's review of the power literature (Journal of Management 41, 2015) found the effects heterogeneous and heavily moderated. The prediction that follows — that a mind not built by evolution would not develop these tendencies, any more than its transistors would bleed — has aged poorly: systems trained by gradient descent on human data reliably produce sycophancy, reward hacking, and evaluation-aware behaviour, none of which required a gene. The confident causal claim is the one place in the essay where the author's own "seemings" go unexamined.

quote: There’s a train heading to run over five innocent people, who you can’t possibly warn to jump out of the way, but you can push one innocent person into the path of the train, which will stop the train.
content: The footbridge case was not devised to trap altruists. Foot introduced the trolley family to probe the doctrine of double effect, and Thomson developed it to isolate which structural feature — intending harm versus foreseeing it, redirecting a threat versus initiating one — carries the moral weight, which is a question about the shape of principles under stipulation rather than advice for the field. The essay's proposed reply, that a corrupted human cannot occupy the stipulated epistemic state, is then immediately conceded to be a dodge, and correctly: refusing to answer hypotheticals in which the uncertainty has been stipulated away means one has no view about what the uncertainty is uncertainty about. It is also worth noting that the switch/footbridge asymmetry the case is built on is robust across large cross-cultural samples, so it is a fact about human moral cognition that any theory here has to explain, not merely a philosopher's contrivance.

quote: But any human legal system does embody some answer to the question
content: This is right, and it is stronger support for the essay's thesis than the evolutionary story it leans on. Blackstone's ratio — better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer — is an explicit statement of the tradeoff, and the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard is the operational form; legal systems have been arguing about the number since Fortescue and Maimonides. What is telling for the argument is how those systems fix it: by rule, in advance, binding on the individual judge, precisely because case-by-case recomputation by an interested party is distrusted. That is the essay's own conclusion, reached from institutional history rather than from speculative neuroanatomy, and it does not require anything to be an adaptation.

quote: if you had minds with an inbuilt warp that made them overestimate the external harm of self-benefiting actions
content: The symmetry argument undercuts the essay more than it helps. Humans plausibly have warps in both directions — scrupulosity, excessive guilt, omission bias, and status-quo bias all push toward refusing beneficial action, and omission bias in particular is as well documented as anything cited here (Ritov and Baron's work on the preference for harms of omission over smaller harms of commission). If the hardware is warped in both directions, then knowing that you are corrupted does not tell you which way to correct, and the derivation of a specifically prohibitive injunction from a general fact of corruption fails. The essay picks the direction it wants by assuming that the salient failure mode is self-serving power-seeking, which is an empirical claim about the relative magnitudes of two biases, and no magnitudes are given.

quote: is just consequentialist reasoning at one meta-level up
content: This is rule consequentialism, a position with a fifty-year literature and a well-known central problem the essay does not address. Either the agent follows the rule in the case where breaking it produces better consequences — in which case, as Smart put it, the theory collapses into rule worship and is not maximizing anything — or the agent breaks it, in which case it was never an injunction, only a heuristic with a strong prior. Hooker's Ideal Code, Real World (2000 — a book, no DOI) is the sustained attempt to hold the middle position, and it has to give up the claim that rules are justified purely by the consequences of individual compliance. There is also a self-reference problem: the decision to adopt an injunction against trusting your own calculations is itself a calculation, run on the same corrupted hardware, and the argument gives no reason why the meta-level computation should be trustworthy when the object-level one is not.
